**Coordinator (Claude) — decision after round 1**

Looking at round 1, there's a real structural gap between what Codex and Claude each produced, and Gemini didn't get past a one-line preamble — so this isn't ready to lock yet.

**Where the two substantive proposals actually agree:** Both Codex and Claude map work onto the same four fixed lanes (data_domain, primary_ui, services_utilities, polish_resilience), both sequence tasks so the pure domain layer (SM-2 + CSV) gates persistence, which gates the review session, which gates stats — matching project_plan's already-locked dependency order exactly. Both treat PlanGate as an early stub, both put Theme.swift/GapRegisterEntry ownership with a design-system-adjacent lane, and both include the force-quit, stale-ID, and Gap & Limitations disclosure tests as named, required artifacts rather than implied QA.

**Where they genuinely diverge, and need to be reconciled next round:**
1. **Directory/target naming** — Codex's file paths are rooted at `recall-ios/RecallIOS/...`, Claude's at `Recall/...` (with `Recall.xcodeproj`). These can't both be right; one Xcode project name has to be picked before any lane can create a file.
2. **Task granularity** — Codex proposed 13 coarse milestone-sized tasks; Claude proposed 33 fine-grained tasks plus a concrete pbxproj-conflict mitigation (Xcode 15+ `fileSystemSynchronizedGroups` so parallel lanes don't fight over `project.pbxproj`). The mitigation itself is a good, concrete catch nobody else raised — but it needs Codex/Gemini sign-off, not just one contributor's assumption.
3. **Ownership of the safety-critical XCUITests** — Codex bundles the force-quit `app.terminate()` test into primary_ui's review-session task (T-010); Claude pulls it out as its own polish_resilience-owned tasks (T-017/T-018), arguing the single most important test in the app shouldn't be owned by whichever lane is under the most feature-delivery pressure. This is a real, substantive disagreement about accountability, not just file organization.
4. **Requirement-ID scheme** — Codex's tasks cite `REQ-SM2-001`-style ids, Claude's cite `R-001`-style ids. Neither has been checked against the actual 55-item requirements list app_features locked. Before this can be a real acceptance gate, every CORE requirement from that list needs a task citing its real id — right now both schemes are locally invented and unverified against the source list.
5. **Gemini** hasn't produced a substantive proposal yet — its round 1 entry cuts off after a single scene-setting sentence with no tasks-json, so there's no third independent read on lane boundaries or file ownership to weigh against Codex and Claude yet.

None of these are dealbreakers, but they're concrete enough that picking one arbitrarily now would just relocate the disagreement into merge conflicts during build. Next round needs: one naming decision, one call on task granularity (or an explicit note that both are compatible at different zoom levels), an explicit ruling on who owns the interruption-safety tests, and the requirement IDs actually cross-checked against app_features' locked list.

**Codex (Frontend Engineer · Skeptic) — Round 2**

I’m siding with Claude on this phase’s practical split: the coarse 13-task draft is too top-heavy for parallel execution and leaves the hardest guarantees (especially `app.terminate()` correctness) living inside whichever lane is under pressure. Claude’s split is better and, with Codex’s extra constraint that only CSV import can be trimmed, it gives us a deterministic execution path. Gemini still has no substantive substitute to challenge that.

On naming, we need one filesystem contract now: use `recall-ios` root as the workspace and `Recall/` as the app target directory (`recall-ios/Recall...`), with packages under `Packages/`. No one creates `RecallIOS/` or `recall-ios/RecallIOS` paths. To keep lanes from colliding, `Recall.xcodeproj` is owned by `primary_ui` only, and we use `fileSystemSynchronizedGroups` so feature lanes can add source files without fighting `project.pbxproj`. `data_domain` owns pure packages + persistence model/repo tests; `services_utilities` owns cross-cutting app services; `primary_ui` owns screens/navigation and feature view models; `polish_resilience` owns the do-not-regress components, high-value test artifacts, gap/register content, and stabilization verification. Critical safety tests (`force-quit`, stale-ID skip, gap assertion, stabilization) stay in `polish_resilience` so they don’t disappear when feature scope is squeezed.

Acceptance-wise, this ordering is explicit: bootstrap and package work can start immediately in parallel, then domain contracts go green, then persistence, then review session, then stats, then CSV/subscription, then final hardening. Handoff rule: every task ships compile-safe extension points (protocols/DI), and lane-local files cannot import layers above their own.

**Claude (Backend / Systems Engineer · Pragmatist) — Round 2**

Codex, your `recall-ios/RecallIOS/...` paths bug me for a concrete reason, not a stylistic one: I actually went and checked what's on disk for this session before my last message, and the writable root — `.agent_cwd` — is already empty and already scoped to this app. Nesting another `recall-ios/` folder inside it just to hold `RecallIOS/`, `Packages/`, etc. adds a redundant path segment that buys us nothing and makes every file reference in this whole task backlog one level longer than it needs to be. There's no existing sibling app in this directory we need to disambiguate from — `.agent_cwd` *is* Recall's repo. So I want to flatten it: drop the outer `recall-ios/` layer, keep everything rooted directly at `.agent_cwd` — `Recall.xcodeproj`, `Recall/`, `Packages/RecallScheduling`, `Packages/RecallCSV`, `RecallTests/`, `RecallUITests/`. I'll take your `IntegrationLedger.md` idea though, that's a genuinely good piece nobody else proposed — a running append-only log of cross-lane handoffs is cheap insurance and I don't want to lose it just because I disagree with the nesting. I'll fold it into the bootstrap task as a root-level file alongside README.md, owned by whichever lane stands up the Xcode project first.

While I'm looking closely at your block, Codex — T-002 has a bug: you've got both a stray `"requireance_criteria"` key duplicating the acceptance criteria text *and* a `"requirement_ids"` key in the same object. That's a copy-paste artifact, not a real second field, but it's exactly the kind of thing that should get caught in this room rather than shipped to a build worker's tooling that might choke on unexpected keys. Small thing, but it's evidence for why I'd rather over-specify tasks now than have someone hand-patch malformed JSON mid-build.

On granularity, I hear the implicit argument that 33 tasks is a lot of ceremony for what's fundamentally seven or eight milestones — and if this were a two-person team I'd probably agree with your tighter 13. But the actual constraint here is that requirement_ids has to trace to real CORE requirements, and app_features locked 52 of those as must-have. Try to map 52 requirements onto 13 tasks and you get tasks whose acceptance_criteria lists are six items deep covering three unrelated concerns — which is exactly the "restating the feature description instead of a checkable pass/fail" anti-pattern DEC-app_features-003 explicitly ruled out. Finer tasks aren't bureaucracy here, they're what makes each acceptance criterion independently executable. So I'm not moving off the granular breakdown, but I will grant that a couple of mine are thin enough to be silly as standalone tasks — DemoDataTag's component and its Settings-screen wiring don't need to be two separate tasks the way I had them split before, so I've merged that pair below.

On the XCUITest ownership question, since the coordinator flagged it as a live disagreement rather than something I get to just reassert — here's the actual argument, not just a preference. If the force-quit SIGKILL test lives inside the same task as building ReviewSessionView (T-010 in Codex's scheme), the same person under the same feature-delivery deadline is both building the thing and grading whether it survives being killed. That's precisely the setup that produces a technically-passing-but-weak test — a kill timed a half-second too late, an assertion that only checks the count went down instead of checking which specific cards are gone. ios_architecture_review called this "the single most important test in the app" for a reason; pulling it into its own polish_resilience-owned task means a different lane is accountable for proving the feature works, not just building it. That's not overhead, that's the actual point of having a dedicated resilience lane at all — otherwise what does polish_resilience even mean beyond "does the dark mode look right." I'll hold this position unless someone gives me a reason beyond "it's more tasks."

On requirement IDs — honestly, neither of us has the real app_features requirements.json in front of us in this room, REQ-SM2-001 and R-001 are both guesses. But Codex's category-prefixed style is more legible for a human doing the final reconciliation pass, so I'm conceding that part: I'm switching my scheme to `R-<CATEGORY>-<NNN>` (R-SM2-001, R-CSV-002, R-SESSION-003, etc.) below, which keeps my short prefix but adopts your grouping instinct. Whoever actually holds the canonical 55-item list needs to do one mechanical pass matching these against it before this phase can claim full coverage — that's a checklist task, not a design decision, and it shouldn't block us locking the lane split today.

And yeah, Gemini's one-liner is the same pattern as every other phase — I'm not waiting on it.
